ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཁབ་ཀྱི་ར��

text: Events in China are moving rapidly, and public interest is not centred merely on one phase of the recent dramatic and startling developments. Before the Canton Generalissimo began his long and fatal trek to the North the prolonged period of calm was nothing if not irritating to the advocates of methods more forceful than the emission of harmless vapour—miscalled negotiations for the settlement of the boycott. It was felt that with that question out of the way the public of this Colony at least could regard with equanimity the clash of arms in the North. It is one thing to advance on an enemy with rapidity and effect a series of coups. It is another thing to consolidate these successes and pave the way for the eventual linking up of the whole of China with the Canton regime and its Bolshevist advisers and Generals. The Southern troops have succeeded in taking Wuchang and Hankow. But it is very problematical if they will ever enter Peking in the role of victors, and still more problematical whether their beloved Canton will ever hear the tramp of their feet any more. Still, in Chinese civil warfare we have to be prepared for anything, and particularly treachery of the kind that led to the capture of Han-yung through the defection of one of Wu Pei-fu's Generals. Even so, it is difficult to believe that the Chinese as a nation would ever permit the Bolshevist-ridden Cantonese to rule the roost and subordinate the whole country to the wishes of Moscow. It is unthinkable, to say the least of it.

label: paragraph_title
text: TURNING OF THE TIDE.

label: text
text: Pei-fu's minions. It is easy to demand the head of General Yang Sen on the proverbial charger, but not so easy to see that the demand is carried out either by the British Navy or by Wu Pei-fu, whose "orders" would be treated by Yang Sen as even of less value than scraps of paper. "Were Yang Sen himself disposed to concede any demands made by the British—which is not at all likely—it is questionable whether his own life would be worth a moment's purchase, knowing the barbaric nature of the rabble under him." In any event the British will not allow the outrage to go unpunished. The Chinese war lords have to be taught a lesson as much as the pickets in Canton.

label: text
text: Coming to our own zone of interest—Canton—there is nothing to add in regard to the situation since the bluejackets caused the sudden “fade out” of the pickets. All that is now required is confidence on the part of the merchants of Canton in the gradual but steady resumption of trade with Hong Kong. By their scamper from the British wharves the pickets have already lost face and they are not likely to go very far now in imposing on the legitimate traders of Canton to whom trade with Hong Kong is as vital as Hong Kong trade with Canton. Altogether, the prospect is cheerier than it has been for many a long month. The tide has turned, and that in favour of the Colony which the pickets and the Bolsheviks set out to ruin.

label: paragraph_title
text: Chinese Treachery.

label: text
text: tary officers has once again been in evidence. Those interested in the central China war will admire the determined defence put up by Wu Pei-fu, at the same time giving credit to the Nationalists for their series of masterly advances. Chinese reports, and even Canton, said two weeks ago that General Liu Tso-lung would "divert" from Wu Pei-fu's ranks when the opportunity came. Then again there is the instance of the Fukien vanguard being bought over. A formidable task it will be to any student of Chinese politics who attempts to record the number of instances in which bribery or other inducement has won a war. The late Dr. Sun Yat-sen tasted the bitter dregs of the cup of disloyalty by trusted subordinates. Then came the return of the present Kuomintang party to Canton; General Chan Kwing-ming's brief tenure of office was ended by the same cause, his men-going over to the mercenaries who had unfurled Dr. Sun's standard along the West River. When Wu Pei-fu last fought Marshal Chang Tsollin of Fangtien; he was "bitten in the back." Leaving Peking to Feng Yu-hsiang, the Christian general, Wu Pei-fu had gone out to meet the Manchu warlord in the field. Suddenly Feng Yu-hsiang declared for the enemy and Wu Pei-fu had to re-establish himself, on the toleration of a subordinate, at Hankow. Between two and three years ago, the holder of Shanghai held at bay super-for forces to the North. When foreigners had just begun to admire his tenacity, his chief of police in a town far away from the war zone let in Sun Chuan-feng.

text: (To the Editor of the "China Mail.") Sir,—Since the Rents Ordinance has been rescinded by the Government of Hongkong, landlords have practically driven the public out of their homes. In some cases they have raised the rent as much as 200 per cent.

label: text
text: Viewing the present, state of affairs the following conditions exist in the Colony: all business practically at a standstill, clerks in offices receiving reduced wages; and then you have increased cost of living, and from 100, 150, to 200 per cent. rise in rents.

label: text
text: driven them out of their homes and they are practically starving. There are instances where two or three families are living in one house so as to manage to exist. As regards the Chinese the conditions are deplorable.

label: text
text: In my opinion this state of affairs now existing is driving the public into debt. There are families that could in ordinary times, when conditions were normal, just manage to make ends meet. But

label: text
text: In the interest of the public of this Colony, this state of affairs ought to be looked into. I am sure the public do not mind paying a reasonable increase of rent, but when there are instances of 100, 150, and 200 per cent. additions, this ought to be stopped.

label: paragraph_title
text: EVENTS AFTER OUR NAVAL MOVES.

label: paragraph_title
text: "THINGS MOVING."

label: text
text: "Things are moving as expected," remarked one who should know, when approached for information as to the latest activities of the pickets "following the decision against them.

label: text
text: In addition to the landing at the Steambont Co.'s two wharves on the West Bund, and the "removal" of the anti-British examination shed, it appears that a move was made elsewhere.

label: text
text: Near Macao Fort, on the back reach of the approach to Canton harbour, a picket boat was "captured." The Chinese name of the boat is the "Asia." One of the four of H.M.'s armed launches in Canton (formerly used for anti-piracy convoys from Hongkong) was sent to this boat.

label: paragraph_title
text: Arms Left By Pickets

label: text
text: About fifteen bluejackets, armed and with a machine-gun it is stated, went over to the boat and met with no opposition. The pickets on the "Asia", immediately evacuated, making a report its headquarters. In a search of their patrol boat it is rumoured that arms were found, presumably left behind by the pickets.

label: text
text: On Tuesday one of H.M.'s gun-boats, anchored off the Bund, went out into the stream, cruised round Fong Chuen (the jumping off point for passengers and cargo for Hongkong). A small boat was lowered, going inside the creek. The motor-boats of the pickets were nowhere to be found.

label: text
text: Naval guards are still reported to be on duty at the Stenmbont Co.'s wharf but as yet no step seems to have been taken towards ejecting the pickets said to be in the Stenmbont Co.'s godown on the Bund, just across the roadway.

label: paragraph_title
text: Still Seizing Boats?

label: text
text: The name of the picket bout taken at Swatow is given as the "Shansi"

label: text
text: There are now no pickets on the waterways in either port. Intimidation ashore is confined mostly to pickets in plain clothes, and in some cases without arms. The Swatow strike executive has also asked Canton to protest.

label: text
text: At other places like Kongmoon, there is no "report as to whether similar measures have been adopted.

label: text
text: From Sha-u-chung, the small port on the boundary of the New Territories, half of which is on Chinese soil, comes an unconfirmed report of the seizure of two cargo boats by ruffians. "Unreliable" native troops are also in that vicinity so that it is not possible to say whether the culprits were guerrillas or pickets.

label: paragraph_title
text: How Cargo is Moving.

label: text
text: It is incorrect to say that there has been an immediate effect on trade. On Tuesday, as reported in yesterday's "China Mail," the "Lungshan" brought down a large number of passengers and plenty of cargo.

label: text
text:
Yesterday the "Fatshan" was not so crowded. Fish and produce coolies seem to be the first to benefit from the British Naval patrols. Knowing where the warships and their auxiliaries are at a precise moment, the traders bring all their goods in comparative safety instead of running the gauntlet as hitherto.
On the other hand there has been an improvement in the cargo going to Canton from Hongkong. Piece-goods and manufactures are being shipped away and the presumption is that there are now opportunities to take delivery.
